text: Winning does not tempt that man. This is how he grows: by being defeated, decisively, by constantly greater beings.
author: Rainer Maria Rilke
locator: The Book of Images; final lines; tr. Robert Bly

text: Real joy, believe me, is a stern matter.
author: Seneca
locator: Letter 23, §4; tr. Richard M. Gummere (Loeb, 1917)

text: If you march your Winter Journeys you will have your reward, so long as all you want is a penguin's egg.
author: Apsley Cherry-Garrard
work: The Worst Journey in the World
locator: Chapter XIX, "Never Again", final sentence of the main text (1922)

text: The crucial thing is to find a truth which is truth for me, to find the idea for which I am willing to live and die.
author: Søren Kierkegaard
locator: Gilleleje, 1 August 1835; Papirer I A 75; tr. Howard V. and Edna H. Hong

text: When you do something, you should burn yourself completely, like a good bonfire, leaving no trace of yourself.
author: Shunryu Suzuki
locator: Part Two, "Right Attitude", chapter "No Trace"

text: The lucidity that was to constitute his torture at the same time crowns his victory. There is no fate that cannot be surmounted by scorn.
author: Albert Camus
locator: Final chapter, "The Myth of Sisyphus"; tr. Justin O'Brien

text: How dull it is to pause, to make an end, / To rust unburnish'd, not to shine in use!
author: Alfred, Lord Tennyson
locator: lines 22–23 (Poems, 1842)

text: You could leave life right now. Let that determine what you do and say and think.
author: Marcus Aurelius
locator: Book 2, §11; tr. Gregory Hays

text: Respect Buddha and the gods without counting on their help.
author: Miyamoto Musashi
locator: Precept 19 of 21 (1645); tr. Kenji Tokitsu / Sherab Chödzin Kohn

text: We run carelessly to the precipice, after we have put something before us to prevent us seeing it.
author: Blaise Pascal
locator: Brunschvicg 183 (Lafuma 166; Sellier 198); tr. W. F. Trotter

text: Philosophy, as I have so far understood and lived it, means living voluntarily among ice and high mountains—seeking out everything strange and questionable in existence, everything so far placed under a ban by morality.
author: Friedrich Nietzsche
locator: Preface, §3; tr. Walter Kaufmann

text: For somewhere there is an ancient enmity / between our daily life and the great work.
author: Rainer Maria Rilke
locator: Near the close of the poem (1908); tr. Stephen Mitchell

text: We took risks, we knew we took them; things have come out against us, and therefore we have no cause for complaint, but bow to the will of Providence, determined still to do our best to the last.
author: Robert Falcon Scott
locator: "Message to the Public", March 1912 (Vol. I, 1913)

text: But all things excellent are as difficult as they are rare.
author: Baruch Spinoza
locator: Part V, Proposition 42, Scholium, final sentence; tr. R. H. M. Elwes

text: We must prefer real hell to an imaginary paradise.
author: Simone Weil
locator: Chapter "Illusions"; tr. Emma Crawford and Mario von der Ruhr

text: The struggle itself toward the heights is enough to fill a man's heart.
author: Albert Camus
locator: Closing paragraph; tr. Justin O'Brien

text: If by setting one's heart right every morning and evening, one is able to live as though his body were already dead, he gains freedom in the Way.
author: Yamamoto Tsunetomo
locator: Chapter 1, the passage beginning "The Way of the Samurai is found in death"; tr. William Scott Wilson

text: He only earns his freedom and existence, / Who daily conquers them anew.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
locator: Act V, Faust's last speech (German ll. 11575–76); tr. Bayard Taylor

text: Whoever has learned to be anxious in the right way has learned the ultimate.
author: Søren Kierkegaard
locator: Chapter V, "Anxiety as Saving through Faith"; tr. Reidar Thomte with Albert B. Anderson

text: Have we vanquished an enemy? None but ourselves. Have we gained success? That word means nothing here.
author: George Leigh Mallory
work: Mont Blanc from the Col du Géant
locator: The Alpine Journal, vol. 32 (1918), p. 162

text: Ivan Ilych's life had been most simple and most ordinary and therefore most terrible.
author: Leo Tolstoy
locator: Chapter II, opening sentence; tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude

text: I judge you unfortunate because you have never been unfortunate; you have passed through life without an antagonist; no one will know what you can do,—not even yourself.
author: Seneca
locator: De Providentia 4.3; tr. John W. Basore (Loeb)

text: Perhaps the nearness of death will bring me the light of life.
author: Ludwig Wittgenstein
locator: MS 103, entry of 4 May 1916; quoted in Ray Monk, Ludwig Wittgenstein: The Duty of Genius (1990), p. 138

text: Shall we be fill'd and satisfied then? / And my spirit said No, we but level that lift to pass and continue beyond.
author: Walt Whitman
locator: Section 46 (Leaves of Grass, 1891–92)

text: Remember that now is the contest, now are the Olympic games, and they cannot be deferred.
author: Epictetus
locator: Chapter 51 (50 in Long's numbering); tr. George Long

text: Courage, however, is the best slayer—courage which attacks: which slays even death itself, for it says, "Was that life? Well then! Once more!"
author: Friedrich Nietzsche
locator: Third Part, "On the Vision and the Riddle", §1; tr. Walter Kaufmann

text: For here there is no place that does not see you. You must change your life.
author: Rainer Maria Rilke
locator: Final lines (New Poems, 1908); tr. Stephen Mitchell

text: I want death to find me planting my cabbages, but careless of death, and still more of my unfinished garden.
author: Michel de Montaigne
locator: Book I, chapter 20, "That to Philosophize Is to Learn to Die"; tr. Donald M. Frame

text: The bow bends; the wood complains. At the moment of supreme tension, there will leap into flight an unswerving arrow, a shaft that is inflexible and free.
author: Albert Camus
locator: Closing lines of "Beyond Nihilism"; tr. Anthony Bower

text: I would hate that death bandaged my eyes and forbore, / And bade me creep past. / No! let me taste the whole of it.
author: Robert Browning
locator: lines 15–17 (Dramatis Personae, 1864)

text: One thing is needful.—To "give style" to one's character—a great and rare art!
author: Friedrich Nietzsche
locator: Book IV, §290; tr. Walter Kaufmann
